abstract: |
  Investors frequently choose to buy into actively managed portfolios in hopes of excess returns in comparison with passive index benchmarks. While many do at certain time periods, it is difficult to isolate whether the excess returns are the result of genuine skill or the randomness in the market. This research aims to test whether a very classical and intuitive strategy - buying the dip - can beat a random portfolio with the same number of buys and sells with statistical significance (α=0.05). Using a Monte Carlo simulation, we create 10,000 portfolios contrained to the same time scope, underlying assets, number of buys/sells and position sizing rules as the buy-the-dip strategy. Comparing the strategy's outcome with this simulated distribution of outcomes will allow us to assess whether its timing signals produce unusually high returns in comparison to the random portfolio benchmark.

1. Data and Assets 

For the purpose of this simulation, daily price data for the SPDR S&P 500 ETF (`SPY`) and NVIDIA (`NVDA`) is examined from January 1, 2016 to January 1, 2026. This time period is appropriate because the market has experienced several macro-shocks such as the 2020 COVID-19 bear market, the 2021 post-pandemic hyper-expansion bull market, the 2023 AI Driven bull market and the 2025 Tariff-Shock bear market. The daily Adjusted Close `Adj Close` will be fetched from the Python library `yfinance` to automatically account for dividends and stock splits.
